lead: A Zener diode is a silicon diode built to work in reverse breakdown. At its breakdown voltage V<sub>Z</sub> the voltage across it stays nearly constant while the current through it changes widely. Put one in parallel with a load, feed both through a series resistor R<sub>s</sub>, and the load sees a steady V<sub>Z</sub> even when the input or load current moves. It is the cheapest way to get a fixed 6 V or 9 V rail, used in small chargers, sensor boards and reference circuits.
prereq: You need: a steady DC input from Chapter 1.2, and diode behaviour from Chapter 1.1.

sections.h3: The Zener works in reverse breakdown

blocks.text: A Zener is a heavily doped silicon p-n junction. Forward biased, it conducts at about 0.7 V like any diode. Reverse biased, it blocks with microamperes of leakage until the reverse voltage reaches V<sub>Z</sub>. At V<sub>Z</sub> the current rises steeply while the voltage across the diode stays almost fixed. It is used reverse biased: forward gives 0.7 V, reverse gives a chosen V<sub>Z</sub> from about 2.4 V to over 100 V.

Below about 5 V the depletion layer is thin and electrons tunnel through it — Zener breakdown. Above about 6 V carriers knock out more carriers — avalanche breakdown. Neither destroys the diode if current is limited and heat is removed.

The reverse characteristic bends at knee current I<sub>Z(min)</sub>. Below it the voltage is not pinned at V<sub>Z</sub>, so there is no regulation. Above it the curve is almost vertical. Data sheets state V<sub>Z</sub> at test current I<sub>ZT</sub>.

blocks.where: r<sub>z</sub> is the dynamic resistance in ohms, ΔV<sub>Z</sub> the small change in Zener voltage in volts and ΔI<sub>Z</sub> the small change in Zener current in amperes. r<sub>z</sub> is a few ohms to tens of ohms, and causes the output to move slightly when current changes.

blocks.text: The regulator has a series resistor R<sub>s</sub> from the input, a Zener from the output node to ground, and the load in parallel with the Zener. The input must be larger than V<sub>Z</sub>. R<sub>s</sub> carries the difference, and whatever current the load does not take flows through the Zener.

I<sub>Rs</sub> = (V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>Z</sub>) / R<sub>s</sub>,   I<sub>Z</sub> = I<sub>Rs</sub> − I<sub>L</sub> = (V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>Z</sub>)/R<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>Z</sub>/R<sub>L</sub>,   P<sub>Z</sub> = V<sub>Z</sub>·I<sub>Z</sub>
blocks.where: V<sub>in</sub> is the DC input in volts, V<sub>Z</sub> the Zener voltage in volts, R<sub>s</sub> the series resistor and R<sub>L</sub> the load resistor, both in ohms; I<sub>Rs</sub>, I<sub>Z</sub> and I<sub>L</sub> are resistor, Zener and load currents in amperes; P<sub>Z</sub> is Zener dissipation in watts.

blocks.text: Regulation holds only while I<sub>Z(min)</sub> ≤ I<sub>Z</sub> ≤ I<sub>Z(max)</sub>. A heavier load lowers I<sub>Z</sub>; below the knee the output sags to V<sub>in</sub>·R<sub>L</sub>/(R<sub>s</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>). A higher input or lighter load raises I<sub>Z</sub>; above I<sub>Z(max)</sub> the Zener overheats.

Line regulation is ΔV<sub>out</sub>/ΔV<sub>in</sub> ≈ r<sub>z</sub>/(R<sub>s</sub> + r<sub>z</sub>) volts per volt; a larger R<sub>s</sub> or smaller r<sub>z</sub> gives a stiffer output. Load regulation is (V<sub>NL</sub> − V<sub>FL</sub>)/V<sub>FL</sub> × 100%, where V<sub>NL</sub> is no-load output and V<sub>FL</sub> full-load output.

sections.h3: Designing R<sub>s</sub> and the power rating

blocks.text: Choose R<sub>s</sub> from the worst case that drains the Zener, then check the case that overloads it.

items: Heaviest load, lowest input: R<sub>s</sub> must still pass I<sub>Z(min)</sub>, so R<sub>s</sub> ≤ (V<sub>in(min)</sub> − V<sub>Z</sub>)/(I<sub>Z(min)</sub> + I<sub>L(max)</sub>), with I<sub>L(max)</sub> = V<sub>Z</sub>/R<sub>L(min)</sub>.
Lightest load, highest input: I<sub>Z(max)</sub> = (V<sub>in(max)</sub> − V<sub>Z</sub>)/R<sub>s</sub> − I<sub>L(min)</sub>, with I<sub>L(min)</sub> = 0 at no load.
Power: P<sub>Z</sub> = V<sub>Z</sub>·I<sub>Z(max)</sub> must stay below the derated rating.
If step 3 fails, use a larger-wattage Zener, a lower V<sub>in(max)</sub>, or a larger R<sub>s</sub> at the cost of load current.

blocks.text: A 1 W Zener rated at 25 °C cannot shed 1 W at 100 °C. Data sheets give linear derating to zero at a maximum junction temperature. If a 1 W part derates to zero at 150 °C, the allowed dissipation at 100 °C is 1 W × (150 − 100)/(150 − 25) = 0.40 W. Design with the derated figure and leave margin for the hottest day inside the cabinet.

figure.caption: The Zener sits in parallel with the load and takes whatever current the load leaves: 27.3 mA flows through R<sub>s</sub>, 6 mA through the 1 kΩ load, and 21.3 mA through the Zener.

spec.title: Zener shunt regulator
spec.aria: Block diagram of a Zener shunt regulator: 12 V input through 220 Ω to a 6 V Zener and 1 kΩ load; the Zener carries 21.3 mA.

examples.question: A Zener shunt regulator has V<sub>in</sub> = 12 V, V<sub>Z</sub> = 6 V, R<sub>s</sub> = 220 Ω and R<sub>L</sub> = 1 kΩ. The Zener needs I<sub>Z</sub> ≥ 5 mA to stay in breakdown. (a) Find the Zener current. (b) Find the Zener power dissipation. (c) Find the smallest load resistance that still keeps I<sub>Z</sub> ≥ 5 mA.
steps: Current through R<sub>s</sub>: I<sub>Rs</sub> = (V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>Z</sub>)/R<sub>s</sub> = (12 − 6)/220 = 0.02727 A = 27.27 mA.
Zener current: I<sub>Z</sub> = I<sub>Rs</sub> − I<sub>L</sub> = 27.27 − 6 = 21.27 mA ≈ 21.3 mA. This is above the 5 mA knee, so the output is regulated.
Zener power: P<sub>Z</sub> = V<sub>Z</sub>·I<sub>Z</sub> = 6 V × 0.02127 A = 0.1276 W = 127.6 mW.
For I<sub>Z</sub> ≥ 5 mA the load may take at most I<sub>L</sub> = 27.27 − 5 = 22.27 mA, so R<sub>L</sub> ≥ V<sub>Z</sub>/I<sub>L</sub> = 6/0.02227 = 269.4 Ω.
Check at R<sub>L</sub> = 269.4 Ω: I<sub>L</sub> = 22.27 mA, I<sub>Z</sub> = 5 mA exactly. Any lower R<sub>L</sub> pushes I<sub>Z</sub> below the knee and the output falls below 6 V.
examples.answer: The Zener carries 21.3 mA and dissipates 127.6 mW; regulation holds only while R<sub>L</sub> ≥ 269.4 Ω at V<sub>in</sub> = 12 V.
examples.check:
Vin = 12.0
Vz = 6.0
Rs = 220.0
RL = 1000.0
Irs = (Vin - Vz) / Rs
IL = Vz / RL
Iz = Irs - IL
Pz = Vz * Iz
print(round(Iz * 1000, 1))
print(round(Pz * 1000, 1))
RLmin = Vz / (Irs - 0.005)
print(round(RLmin, 1))

traps: Claiming V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>Z</sub> when I<sub>Z</sub> is below I<sub>Z(min)</sub>. Check current first; otherwise output is the divider V<sub>in</sub>·R<sub>L</sub>/(R<sub>s</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>).
Ignoring Zener power. At no load the Zener carries the whole (V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>Z</sub>)/R<sub>s</sub>, which is where it burns.
Reversing the load limit: a smaller R<sub>L</sub> draws more current and starves the Zener, so the design check gives a minimum R<sub>L</sub>, not a maximum.
Designing with nominal 12 V instead of V<sub>in(min)</sub> and V<sub>in(max)</sub>. Mains and transformer outputs swing by ±10% or more; worst cases sit at opposite ends.
Mixing V<sub>Z</sub> with r<sub>z</sub>. V<sub>Z</sub> sets the output level; only r<sub>z</sub> decides how much the output moves when current changes.

quiz.q: Define I<sub>Z(min)</sub> and state what goes wrong below it.
quiz.a: I<sub>Z(min)</sub> is the knee current of the reverse characteristic, below which voltage is not clamped at V<sub>Z</sub>. The Zener acts almost as an open circuit and output collapses to V<sub>in</sub>·R<sub>L</sub>/(R<sub>s</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>).

quiz.q: With V<sub>in</sub> = 12 V, R<sub>s</sub> = 220 Ω and V<sub>Z</sub> = 6 V, load current jumps from 6 mA to 20 mA. What happens at the output?
quiz.a: I<sub>Rs</sub> stays at 27.3 mA, so I<sub>Z</sub> falls from 21.3 mA to 7.3 mA. It is still above the 5 mA knee, so output drops only by r<sub>z</sub> × 14 mA, tens of millivolts. At a load of 27.3 mA, I<sub>Z</sub> reaches zero and regulation ends.

quiz.q: A regulator has V<sub>in</sub> = 15 V, V<sub>Z</sub> = 9 V, R<sub>s</sub> = 300 Ω and R<sub>L</sub> = 1.5 kΩ. Find I<sub>Z</sub> and P<sub>Z</sub>.
quiz.a: I<sub>Rs</sub> = (15 − 9)/300 = 20 mA. I<sub>L</sub> = 9/1500 = 6 mA. I<sub>Z</sub> = 20 − 6 = 14 mA. P<sub>Z</sub> = 9 V × 14 mA = 126 mW.

quiz.q: A 1 W Zener derates linearly to zero at 150 °C. What power may it dissipate at 75 °C?
quiz.a: Fraction left = (150 − 75)/(150 − 25) = 75/125 = 0.6, so allowed dissipation is 1 W × 0.6 = 0.60 W.

quiz.q: Why can a small R<sub>s</sub> destroy the Zener at no load while the circuit looks fine with the load connected?
quiz.a: At no load I<sub>Z</sub> = (V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>Z</sub>)/R<sub>s</sub>, which is largest when the load is removed. A small R<sub>s</sub> makes this current large, so P<sub>Z</sub> = V<sub>Z</sub>·I<sub>Z</sub> exceeds the rating. With the load connected, part of the current goes to the load and the fault stays hidden.

quiz.q: A student measures 5.2 V instead of the expected 6 V and blames the Zener. Give two other explanations.
quiz.a: Either I<sub>Z</sub> is below I<sub>Z(min)</sub> — load too heavy, R<sub>s</sub> too large, or V<sub>in</sub> too low — or the part is a 5.1 V Zener misread as 6 V. Check V<sub>in</sub>, R<sub>L</sub> and the part marking before replacing the diode.

quiz.q: Why does a larger R<sub>s</sub> improve line regulation but reduce the load the circuit can serve?
quiz.a: Line regulation is about r<sub>z</sub>/(R<sub>s</sub> + r<sub>z</sub>), so a larger R<sub>s</sub> makes output stiffer against input changes. But it leaves less current after supplying I<sub>Z(min)</sub>, so the heaviest load current, (V<sub>in(min)</sub> − V<sub>Z</sub>)/R<sub>s</sub> − I<sub>Z(min)</sub>, shrinks.

beyond: Not for the exam. Below about 5 V a Zener has a negative temperature coefficient and above about 6 V a positive one; near 5.6 V the two nearly cancel, which is why 5.6 V parts were once popular as references. Modern designs use bandgap and buried-Zener references, or a TL431 shunt regulator, when drift of tens of ppm matters.
